Description: anti-pattern — porting a Native font-faces config to GL JS
prompt: I have a working `font-faces` config in my MapLibre Native app's stylesheet that renders local fonts offline with explicit Unicode ranges per file. I'm now building a MapLibre GL JS web app and want the same offline-font behavior — can I copy the same `font-faces` config into my GL JS stylesheet?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
No – the `font-faces` block that you use in a MapLibre Native style (C++/mobile) cannot be copied verbatim into a MapLibre GL JS style and expect the same “offline-font” behaviour.  

MapLibre GL JS does not read local font files directly from the stylesheet. Instead it always asks a **glyph server** (the URL you put in the top-level `glyphs` property) for the glyphs it needs, and the server returns them as **PBF** tiles. The `font-faces` object is a native-only construct that tells the native runtime how to map a logical font name to a set of local `.ttf/.otf` files and which Unicode ranges belong to each file.

Below you’ll find a concise explanation of why the native config can’t be reused, followed by the practical ways you can achieve the same “offline-font” experience in a web app.

---

## 1️⃣ Why the native `font-faces` block doesn’t work in GL JS

| Feature | MapLibre Native | MapLibre GL JS (browser) |
|---------|----------------|--------------------------|
| **Font source** | Local `.ttf/.otf` files referenced in `font-faces` | Glyphs are fetched from a URL (`glyphs`) that returns vector-glyph PBFs |
| **Unicode-range handling** | You can split a logical font into several files, each with its own `unicode-range` | The glyph server decides which glyphs belong to which font; the style only lists font families in `text-font` |
| **Offline guarantee** | The app ships the font files, so no network request is needed | The browser can only load what the server serves over HTTP(S). A `file://` URL is blocked by most browsers, and there is no built-in fallback to local files. |
| **Style syntax** | `font-faces` is a top-level object in the style JSON | Not part of the GL JS style spec – the spec only defines `glyphs`, `sprite`, `sources`, `layers`, etc. |

Because GL JS never looks at `font-faces`, copying that block will simply be ignored. The only thing GL JS cares about is the `glyphs` URL and the `text-font` array you set on each text layer.

---

## 2️⃣ How to get “offline fonts” in a MapLibre GL JS web app

### 2️⃣.1 Serve your own glyph PBFs locally

1. **Generate glyph PBFs**  
   Use the **Mapbox GL Native glyph server** (the same binary that ships with MapLibre Native) or the open-source **`tilelive-font`** / **`fontnik`** pipeline to turn your `.ttf/.otf` files into the PBF format that GL JS expects.

   ```bash
   # Example with the MapLibre Native glyph server (Docker)
   docker run -v $(pwd)/fonts:/fonts -p 8080:80 maplibre/maplibre-native-glyphs \
       --fonts /fonts --output /glyphs
   ```

   This will create a directory structure like:

   ```
   /glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf
   ```

2. **Host the glyph directory**  
   Run a tiny static-file server (e.g., `python -m http.server`, `serve`, `nginx`, etc.) that makes the `glyphs` folder reachable via HTTP.

   ```bash
   cd glyphs
   python -m http.server 8000
   ```

3. **Point your GL JS style at the local server**  

   ```json
   {
     "version": 8,
     "glyphs": "http://localhost:8000/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
     "layers": [...]
   }
   ```

   Because the glyphs are now served from `localhost`, the app works completely offline (as long as the server is running).

### 2️⃣.2 Split fonts by Unicode range (optional)

If you want the same optimisation you had in native—different files for Latin, CJK, Emoji, etc.—you can still do it, but you have to **pre-split the fonts before generating the PBFs**. The glyph server will treat each font family (fontstack) as a single logical name, so you would:

| Desired logical name | Physical file(s) |
|----------------------|------------------|
| `MyFont` (Latin)     | `MyFont-Latin.ttf` |
| `MyFont` (CJK)       | `MyFont-CJK.ttf`   |
| `MyFont` (Emoji)     | `MyFont-Emoji.ttf` |

When you run the glyph generator, give it **all** the files under the same family name (`MyFont`). The generator will automatically merge the Unicode ranges from each file into the appropriate PBF tiles. The result is a single glyph stack (`MyFont`) that contains all the glyphs you need, but the underlying source files are still split.

### 2️⃣.3 Use a “data-uri” fallback (experimental)

A few developers have tried to embed a **complete glyph PBF** as a data URI in the `glyphs` property, e.g.:

```json
"glyphs": "data:application/x-protobuf;base64,AAAA...."
```

This works only for **one** glyph range (the `{range}` placeholder cannot be used) and quickly becomes impractical for a full-language set. It’s not recommended for production.

### 2️⃣.4 Alternative: Use the `fontstack` CSS trick (not offline)

If you are okay with the browser loading system fonts (or web-fonts) via CSS `@font-face`, you can style your map text with **CSS** instead of the GL JS glyph pipeline, but you lose the ability to use MapLibre’s layout features (e.g., `text-transform`, `text-letter-spacing`) on those characters. This approach is **not** an offline solution because the browser still needs to download the font files.

---

## 3️⃣ Step-by-step recipe for a typical offline web map

Below is a concrete checklist you can follow:

| Step | Command / Action | Result |
|------|------------------|--------|
| **1. Gather fonts** | `MyFont-Latin.ttf`, `MyFont-CJK.ttf`, `MyFont-Emoji.ttf` | All glyphs you need, split by Unicode range (optional). |
| **2. Install glyph server** | `npm i -g @maplibre/maplibre-gl-native-glyphs` *(or use Docker image)* | Binary that converts TTF/OTF → PBF. |
| **3. Generate glyphs** | `maplibre-gl-native-glyphs --fonts ./fonts --output ./glyphs` | Creates `glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`. |
| **4. Serve them** | `npx serve ./glyphs -l 8080` (or any static server) | HTTP endpoint reachable at `http://localhost:8080`. |
| **5. Edit your style** | ```json "glyphs": "http://localhost:8080/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf" ``` | GL JS will request glyphs from the local server. |
| **6. Deploy** | Bundle the static server with your web app (e.g., as part of a Node/Express backend, or as a Service Worker cache) | Users can load the map without any external network request. |

**Tip:** If you want the whole thing to be a *single* HTML file (e.g., for a demo), you can pre-bundle the glyph PBFs into a **Service Worker cache** at install time. The Service Worker intercepts requests to `http://myapp.local/glyphs/...` and serves the cached binary blobs. This still requires a tiny bit of JavaScript, but it keeps the user completely offline after the first load.

---

## 4️⃣ Frequently asked follow-ups

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| *Can I just copy the `font-faces` JSON into the GL JS style and expect it to work?* | No. GL JS ignores `font-faces`. Only the `glyphs` URL matters. |
| *Do I need to rebuild the glyphs every time I add a new character?* | Yes. Glyph PBFs are generated per Unicode range (e.g., `0-255`, `256-511`, …). Adding a new character that falls into a range you already have will be served automatically; adding a character in a new range requires regenerating that range’s PBF. |
| *What about Mapbox-compatible styles that already point to `https://api.mapbox.com/fonts/v1/...`?* | Replace that URL with your local server URL. The format (`{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`) is identical. |
| *Can I use the same `unicode-range` syntax in GL JS?* | No. The `unicode-range` property lives only in the native `font-faces` block. In GL JS you control the ranges by how you split the source TTF/OTF files before generating the glyph PBFs. |
| *Is there a CDN that hosts the PBF glyphs for me?* | MapLibre does not provide an official CDN. You can host them on any static file host (GitHub Pages, Netlify, S3, Cloudflare R2, etc.) as long as the URL pattern matches `{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`. |
| *Will this work on mobile browsers?* | Absolutely – as long as the glyph files are reachable via HTTP(S) (or via a Service Worker cache). No native code is required. |

---

## 5️⃣ TL;DR Summary

* **Copy-paste `font-faces` → No.** GL JS does not read that block.
* **Offline fonts in GL JS = Serve glyph PBFs locally.**  
  1. Convert your `.ttf/.otf` files (optionally split by Unicode range) to the PBF format using the MapLibre glyph server.  
  2. Host the resulting `glyphs/…` directory on a local/static HTTP server (or bundle it in a Service Worker).  
  3. Point the style’s top-level `glyphs` property at that server (`http://localhost:…/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`).
* **Unicode-range optimisation** is still possible, but you do it **before** generating the glyphs, not via a `unicode-range` field in the style.

If you follow the steps above you’ll get the same “offline-only, fast, deterministic font rendering” that you enjoy in MapLibre Native, now in a browser-based MapLibre GL JS application. Happy mapping!
Grader Reason: The output incorrectly states that MapLibre GL JS does not support the `font-faces` block and that it ignores it. The rubric explicitly states that the output should NOT claim this, as newer versions of MapLibre GL JS (>= 6.7.0) do support `font-faces`.

## TL;DR  

The problem isn’t the **font** – it’s the **glyph server**.  
MapLibre GL JS does **no text-shaping** itself; it expects the glyphs that come from the `{glyphs}` endpoint to already be *pre-shaped* (i.e. the “final” glyph for every Unicode code-point sequence).  

If you point the style at a server that simply returns the raw TrueType/OTF outlines (one glyph per code-point) you will see exactly what you described: every vowel sign, virama, or conjunct is drawn as a separate character and ends up in the wrong place.

The fix is to use a glyph server that runs HarfBuzz (or another shaping engine) on-the-fly, or to generate a **shaped glyph-pbf** set yourself and serve that.  

Below is a step-by-step guide to get Hindi (Devanagari) labels looking correct with MapLibre GL JS.

---

## 1. Understand the data flow

| Step | What happens | Who does it |
|------|--------------|-------------|
| **A** | MapLibre reads the style → finds the `glyphs` URL (e.g. `https://myserver.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`). | MapLibre JS |
| **B** | When a label is drawn, MapLibre asks the glyph server for the *range* that contains the needed code-points. | Glyph server |
| **C** | The glyph server **must** return a *shaped* SDF glyph for each *character cluster* (e.g. `क्` + `ष` → `क्ष`). | Glyph server (HarfBuzz) |
| **D** | MapLibre draws the SDF glyphs, positions them, and you get a correctly-shaped label. | MapLibre JS |

If step **C** is missing shaping, you get the “each letter on its own” artefact.

---

## 2. Choose a shaping-aware glyph server

| Option | How to get it | Pros | Cons |
|--------|---------------|------|------|
| **Mapbox’s official glyph server** (`https://api.mapbox.com/fonts/v1/{username}/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`) | Requires a Mapbox token (free tier works). | Fully tested, handles all complex scripts out-of-the-box. | You need a Mapbox account; usage limits apply. |

### 3.1 Install the server

```bash

npm install -g @mapbox/mbgl-glyphs
```

> The package is a thin wrapper around the C++ glyph server used by Mapbox GL Native. It ships with HarfBuzz, so it will shape Devanagari correctly.

### 3.2 Prepare the font

Download the exact font file you want to use (e.g. Noto Sans Devanagari Regular).

```bash

cd fonts
wget https://github.com/googlefonts/noto-fonts/raw/main/hinted/ttf/NotoSansDevanagari/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf
```

### 3.3 Run the server

```bash

mbgl-glyphs \
  --font-directory ./fonts \
  --port 8080 \
  --cache-size 500   # MB, optional
```

You should see something like:

```
Listening on http://0.0.0.0:8080
```

The server now answers requests such as:

> **Tip:** The server automatically normalises the `fontstack` name (spaces become `%20`). Use the exact name that appears in your style’s `text-font` array.

```json
  "layers": [

      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
```

* Open DevTools → Application → Clear storage → “Clear site data”, **or**
* Append a cache-busting query string to the glyph URL (e.g. `?v=2`) and reload.

## 5. Why the “raw glyph” approach fails for Hindi

Devanagari (and many other Indic scripts) uses **complex shaping**:

* **Vowel signs** (`ा`, `ि`, `ी`, `ु`, `ू`, `े`, `ै`, `ो`, `ौ`) are *combining marks* that attach to the base consonant.
* The **virama** (`्`) can suppress the inherent vowel and trigger a **conjunct** (ligature) with the following consonant.
* Some consonant clusters have *pre-base* or *post-base* forms (e.g. `र्` + `य` → `र्य`).

All of this is encoded in the **GSUB** (Glyph Substitution) and **GPOS** (Glyph Positioning) tables of the OpenType font. A glyph server that merely extracts the outline for each Unicode code-point never looks at those tables, so each component is drawn independently and ends up “floating”.

MapLibre GL JS deliberately off-loads shaping to the glyph server because shaping is CPU-intensive and because the SDF pipeline expects a *single* glyph per cluster. The server you were using (likely a simple static-file server) didn’t run HarfBuzz, so you got the un-shaped result.

## 1️⃣ Why the “raw-glyph” server breaks Devanagari

When you use the demo glyph URL that ships with the MapLibre starter kit:

```json
"glyphs": "https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf"
```

the server simply extracts the *outline* for each Unicode code-point from the TTF/OTF and puts it into a PBF. No **GSUB** (Glyph Substitution) table is consulted, so:

* `क` (U+0915) → rendered correctly (single glyph)
* `कि` (U+0915 U+093F) → rendered as two separate glyphs: a base “ka” and a detached “i-matra” that sits to the right of the *next* character instead of on top of the “ka”.

Devanagari, like many Indic scripts, relies on **contextual shaping** (conjuncts, vowel signs, reordering). The only way to get the correct visual result is to let a shaping engine (HarfBuzz) apply the GSUB rules **before** the glyphs are turned into a PBF.

MapLibre GL JS does not ship HarfBuzz because it would add a heavy dependency to the browser bundle. Instead it delegates the work to the glyph server.

```bash
done
```
